title: Bit-Counting Tricks — Brian Kernighan's Algorithm and Popcount
summary: Counting set bits fast starts with one identity — n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit. That single trick powers Brian Kernighan's popcount loop, power-of-two checks, and a family of subset-cardinality tricks worth recognizing on sight.

slides.markdown:
How many bits are set in this integer? It sounds like a scan-every-bit question, and the naive answer — shift and check 32 or 64 times — works, but it does the same amount of work whether the number has 1 set bit or 63.

**Brian Kernighan's trick** does better: it costs one iteration *per set bit*, not per bit of width. A number with only 2 bits set finishes in 2 iterations, no matter whether it's a 32-bit or 64-bit integer. That single identity — `n & (n-1)` clears exactly the lowest set bit — is the whole mechanism, and it shows up constantly: population-count instructions, sparse bitsets, Hamming-distance checks, and power-of-two tests all lean on it.

This topic is that identity, the loop it builds, a faster relative (`n & -n`), and the honest trade-off against just calling a built-in.

slides.sectionTitle: Why n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit
slides.markdown:
Take any integer `n` with at least one set bit. Look at its lowest set bit — call its position `k`. Every bit below `k` is 0.

Subtracting 1 borrows from that lowest set bit: bit `k` flips from 1 to 0, and every bit *below* `k` flips from 0 to 1 (that's how borrowing works in binary — same reason `100 - 1 = 011`). Bits *above* `k` are untouched.

So `n` and `n - 1` agree everywhere above bit `k`, disagree exactly at bit `k`, and are exact opposites below it. ANDing them together: the bits above `k` pass through unchanged (matching bits AND to themselves), bit `k` becomes 0 (1 AND 0), and the bits below `k` become 0 (each is 0 AND 1, or equivalently the opposite pair ANDs to 0).

Net effect: **`n & (n-1)` is `n` with its single lowest set bit turned off, and nothing else changed.**

slides.sectionTitle: Peeling bits one at a time
slides.subTitle: A worked trace on n = 44
slides.markdown:
Trace it on `n = 44` (binary `101100`):

- `101100 & 101011` (that's `44 & 43`) → `101000` — the lowest set bit (position 2) is gone.
- `101000 & 100111` (that's `40 & 39`) → `100000` — the next lowest set bit (position 3) is gone.
- `100000 & 011111` (that's `32 & 31`) → `000000` — the last set bit (position 5) is gone, and `n` is now 0.

Three set bits, three iterations, done — regardless of whether `n` is stored in 8, 32, or 64 bits. A number with only its top bit set (like `100000...0`) still finishes in one iteration, even though a naive shift-and-check loop would run the full bit width.

slides.subTitle: O(number of set bits), not O(bit width)
slides.markdown:
The loop just repeats the clear-lowest-bit step and counts how many times it ran:

```python
def popcount(n: int) -> int:
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= n - 1   # clear the lowest set bit
        count += 1
    return count
```

Compare that to the naive version, which always runs once per bit of the type's width:

```python
def popcount_naive(n: int) -> int:
    count = 0
    while n:
        count += n & 1
        n >>= 1
    return count
```

Both are correct. The naive loop runs 32 or 64 times regardless of how sparse `n` is. Kernighan's loop runs once per *set* bit — for a number like `0x80000000` (one bit set, in a 32-bit word) that's the difference between 1 iteration and 32.

slides.subTitle: A related but different trick
slides.markdown:
`n & (n-1)` **removes** the lowest set bit. Its close cousin, `n & -n`, does the opposite: it **isolates** the lowest set bit, leaving every other bit zero.

Why it works: in two's complement, `-n` is `~n + 1`. `~n` flips every bit of `n`, and adding 1 ripples that flip back through all the bits below the original lowest set bit — so below that position, `-n` matches `n` exactly, and above it, `-n` is the exact complement. ANDing `n` with `-n` keeps only the position where both agree on a 1: the lowest set bit, alone.

On `n = 44` (`101100`), `n & -n` gives `000100` (that's 4) — the lowest set bit as a standalone value, not a position index. This is the core primitive behind a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree), where `i & -i` finds the size of the range a given index is responsible for.

A power of two has **exactly one** set bit (`1`, `10`, `100`, `1000`, …). Clearing that one bit with `n & (n-1)` should leave nothing — so checking for zero afterward tells you the answer without ever counting bits:

```python
def is_power_of_two(n: int) -> bool:
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0
```

The `n > 0` guard matters: without it, `n = 0` passes (`0 & -1 == 0` in a two's-complement sense) and falsely reports a power of two, even though zero has no set bits at all — it's a special case the identity doesn't cover on its own.

This one-liner shows up constantly outside puzzle questions: capacity checks for hash-table resizing (which typically round up to a power of two), alignment checks in memory allocators, and validating that a buffer size is a clean power-of-two block.

slides.sectionTitle: Kernighan's loop vs a built-in vs a lookup table
slides.markdown:
Three ways to count set bits, with different trade-offs:

| Approach | Time | When it wins |
|---|---|---|
| **Kernighan's loop** | O(number of set bits) | No built-in available, or the language/interviewer wants the mechanism shown |
| **Built-in popcount** (`bin(n).count("1")` in Python, `Integer.bitCount` in Java, `__builtin_popcount` in C++, or the hardware `POPCNT` instruction) | O(1) effectively | Production code — it compiles to a single CPU instruction on modern hardware and is both faster and harder to get wrong |
| **Precomputed lookup table** (e.g. popcount of every byte 0–255, combined 4 bytes at a time) | O(1) per byte, O(word size / 8) total | Extremely hot loops on hardware or in a language without a fast built-in, at the cost of memory and setup |

In an interview, lead with Kernighan's loop to show you understand *why* it's fast, then mention that production code reaches for the built-in — most languages compile it straight to a single `POPCNT` instruction, which no hand-rolled loop can beat.

Both the Kernighan popcount loop and the power-of-two check rely on the `while n` / `n > 0` guard, and skipping it is the single most common bug in this family.

- **Popcount:** `while n:` correctly exits immediately when `n = 0`, returning 0 — there are no set bits to clear. This one is usually fine because the loop condition naturally covers it.
- **Power-of-two check:** this is the one that bites. `(n & (n - 1)) == 0` is true for `n = 0` (there's no bit to clear, so the AND is trivially 0), but zero is **not** a power of two. Forgetting the explicit `n > 0` guard silently reports `is_power_of_two(0) == True`.

A second, related trap: applying either trick to a **negative** number under two's complement. `n & (n - 1)` and `n & -n` are defined in terms of bit patterns, and a negative number's leading bits are all 1s — the loop will still terminate (eventually the last 1 bit clears), but "how many set bits does -1 have" is a question that depends on the integer's bit width, which is easy to get wrong across languages with fixed-width versus arbitrary-precision integers.

"O(number of set bits)" is a data-dependent bound, not a fixed one — and that distinction is worth being precise about in an interview.

- **Worst case:** a number with every bit set (e.g. `0xFFFFFFFF`) still takes 32 iterations — Kernighan's loop degrades to the same cost as the naive shift-and-check loop when the input is dense.
- **Best case:** a number with one bit set finishes in a single iteration regardless of bit width.
- **The real win is on sparse inputs.** If you're counting bits across many values and most of them are sparse — a common shape in bitset-based problems — Kernighan's loop pays only for the bits that are actually there, while the naive loop always pays for the full width.

The honest framing: Kernighan's trick is never *asymptotically worse* than the naive scan, and is strictly better whenever the input isn't fully dense. That's a safe default to reach for even when you don't know the bit density in advance.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up outside interviews
slides.markdown:
Bit-counting isn't just a puzzle-question staple — it's load-bearing in real systems:

- **Hamming distance / error-correcting codes:** the number of differing bits between two values is `popcount(a ^ b)` — used to measure signal corruption and in nearest-neighbor search over binary hashes (e.g. locality-sensitive hashing for image or document similarity).
- **Bitset cardinality:** databases and search engines (Roaring Bitmaps, PostgreSQL's bitmap index scans) represent row sets as bitsets, and "how many rows match" is a popcount over the whole bitset.
- **Hardware support:** x86's `POPCNT`, ARM's `VCNT`, and most CPUs since roughly 2008 implement population count as a single instruction — a strong signal that this operation was common and expensive enough to earn silicon.
- **Fenwick trees / binary indexed trees:** `i & -i` (from the previous slide) is the core step in both updating and querying a Fenwick tree in O(log n).

Recognizing "this reduces to a popcount" is often the harder half of these problems — the loop itself is three lines.

slides.sectionTitle: From counting bits to enumerating them
slides.markdown:
Everything so far treats an integer as a bag of bits you count or clear one at a time. The next step up is treating an integer as a **representation of a whole set** — bit `i` set means "item `i` is in this subset."

That reframing is where bit tricks stop being isolated puzzle answers and start being a modeling tool: once a subset is just an integer, enumerating all subsets of a small collection, checking membership, and building a dynamic-programming state out of "which items have I used so far" all become integer operations instead of data-structure operations.

That's the subject of the next topic in this group.
